TL;DR for the pomodoro method:

There are five basic steps to implementing the technique:

Decide on the task to be done
Set the pomodoro timer to n minutes (traditionally 25)[1]
Work on the task until the timer rings; record with an x
Take a short break (3–5 minutes)
After four pomodori, take a longer break (15–30 minutes)

I studied accounting and business finance which actually had a lot of contextual papers and journals I had to read, so I would sit down, skim over the paper first to get the gist or the main points, then read it a second time slightly more deliberately to fill in a google docs template to look like this; (example is from my notes)

The contingent design of performance measurement
Robert Chenhall (2006)

Summary
Chenhall looks at performance measurement evolutions and how they are useful in organisations. He finds that enhanced performance from new performance measures depends on the organisational context.

Introduction
Performance measurement is at the heart of control. Traditionally these have been monetary measures. Many management accountants have called for more specific measures that incorporate non-financial information. Chenhall sets out to suggest that enhanced performance outcomes from using non-financial information depends on the organisational context.

Interesting points
Contingency approaches see organisations change their approaches over time to fit new contingencies.

Contextual variables: external environment; strategy; technology; organisational structure; size.

There have been many innovations in performance measurement.

Non financial measures, integrated measures, contingencies affecting integrated measures.

Conclusion
i. It is unlikely that these innovations will be useful in all organisations - it was found that positive benefits are not universalistic.
ii. Performance measures should be considered in the broader patterns of organisational context
iii. Suggested that innovative perfomance measures are ‘fads and fashions’ rather than having genuine improvements across the board - firms just want to appear like they are using the most contemporary measures

Then I could move onto the next paper, it would take me about two hours to do each one, and I'd put some time apart at the end of the week to skim over previous weeks works to tie them together and allow my brain to make connections between different pieces of work. In this way I was very task focused, being able to do a 'job' of study then move onto the next paper to study, rather than thinking of it in half hour blocks. It worked for me :).

It depends on what you're studying, but if it has to do with memorizing things (like history, psychology, etc.) then I've found splitting things into little tiny chunks and memorizing the chunks while splicing in recall always works. Let's say you need to learn various dates and what happened:

  • Study date A until you can recall it with no outside help.

  • Study date B until you can recall it with no outside help.

  • GO BACK TO DATE A and see if you can still recall it.

  • Study date C until you can recall it with no outside help.

  • GO BACK TO DATE B and see if you can still recall it.

It seems to help when recalling things after learning new information, instead of just repeating them after learning them (like when using flashcards). It also helps limit the times you have to go back to a certain part, because you're constantly recalling all the separate pieces. Don't know if this tactic has it's own name or not, just know that it really works for me.

I like the idea of the pomodoro method, I've always incorporated breaks but I've never done them at defined intervals like that.

First, I like to get a strong cup of coffee and throw on some ambient music, either instrumental or in another language. I like Sigur Ros and Tujiko Noriko a lot for focusing.

Next, depending on the nature of what I'm studying I'll make an outline and/or draw diagrams. I've found that writing things down helps me remember them. If it's a complex diagram like memorizing types of reactions in organic chemistry, I'll draw it over and over again doing as much as I can by memory. Even if you're just reading through something, especially a scientific text, take a moment to stop, close your eyes and think about the process you're reading about to be sure that you really understand it.

Last, some things are just straight up memorization. If I have to remember, for example, a bunch of disease states in pathophysiology and the basic idea behind what they do, I use the Method of loci. I was iffy about it when I first tried it, but it really, really works for things that are just memorization as opposed to understanding some sort of process.

associative learning is the only thing that works really reliably for me.

here is an example:

in swahili, the word for fruit is matunda.

to remember this, picture a few pieces of fruit, sitting on top of a mat (such as a welcome mat for a doorway). visualize the doorway, the welcome mat, and the fruit sitting on top of the mat. picture it in your head for 10 seconds. the mat is under the fruit. matunda = mat under

you'll never forget that now. it's hard to apply to all scenarios, but it is something to keep in mind.

You may have already heard of the memory palace idea. The basic premise is that you want to remember pictures and places associated with what you're memorizing. Our brains aren't good at storing boring and uninteresting stuff.

If I needed to memorize a bunch of boring facts, I would find a way to picture the information in the most ridiculous way, or tie it to a physical object mentally.
